items.title: CMA CGM completes $1.4bn FedEx Supply Chain takeover
items.original_title: CMA CGM completes $1.4bn FedEx Supply Chain takeover
items.summary: CMA CGM announced today that it has completed its $1.4bn takeover of FedEx’s contract logistics business, FedEx Supply Chain, which is set to be folded into the shipping line’s contract logistics arm Ceva. The deal will see Ceva’s North American footprint almost treble in size, according to CMA CGM, with the addition of around 34m sqft of warehouse space offering combined operations across 150 warehouses in region and employing around 20,000 staff. “The completion of this acquisition marks an important step in the development of CMA CGM and CEVA Logistics in North America,” Rodolphe Saadé, chairman and chief executive of the CMA CGM group, said. “By significantly expanding our contract logistics capabilities, we are strengthening our ability to offer customers integrated, end-to-end supply chain solutions across ocean, air, land and logistics. “It also reinforces CMA CGM’s long-term commitment to investing in the United States, a strategic growth market for the group, and supporting the resilience and efficiency of its supply chain,” he added. The deal is central to Mr Saadé’s strategy of expanding CMA CGM’s less-cyclical logistics activities. An additional clause in the deal also sees FedEx “enter into multi-year commercial agreements” with CMA CGM’s ocean freight operations and CMA CGM Air Cargo.

items.title: Precious adds Asyad deal to ultramax fixing run
items.original_title: Precious adds Asyad deal to ultramax fixing run
items.summary: Thai dry bulk owner Precious Shipping has fixed its recently delivered ultramax Rossarin Naree to Asyad Shipping for up to 14 months in the latest index-linked deal for its larger bulker fleet. The Khalid Hashim-led company said the 63,500 dwt ship started a 12-to-14-month charter with Asyad on October 1 at a gross variable rate equivalent to 108% of the Baltic Exchange Supramax Index 63K weighted time-charter average over the preceding 15 days. Precious put the current equivalent rate at around $24,000 per day. The Rossarin Naree joined the fleet from China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering at the end of May as the first in a four-ship ultramax series ordered in 2024 for a combined $133.46m, or about $33.36m apiece. Newly delivered sistership Ratima Naree went straight to Trafigura Maritime Logistics last month for 12 to 14 months at 107.5% of the BSI 63K, equivalent to around $22,800 per day when the charter started. A couple of weeks later, the 2016-built ultramax Sunisa Naree was fixed to Singapore’s PACC Line for 11 to 13 months at 103% of the same index, then equivalent to about $23,000 per day. The fixture comes as Precious continues to expand its ultramax exposure.

items.title: Rio Tinto sell-down spreads to post-panamaxes
items.original_title: Rio Tinto sell-down spreads to post-panamaxes
items.summary: Rio Tinto’s owned-vessel sell-down appears to be extending beyond the newcastlemax fleet it cleared out this year, with a pair of 2013-built post-panamax bulkers reported sold en bloc for $42.8m. Broker reports list the 89,892 dwt RTM Dias and RTM Flinders , both built by Namura in Japan, at $21.4m each. The ships are part of Rio Tinto’s owned shipping operation. RTM Dias was delivered by Namura to Rio Tinto Shipping in 2013, while current fleet records list RTM Flinders under Rio Tinto Shipping Asia ownership and Rio Tinto Shipping management. The deal is separate from the newcastlemax sell-down Splash has tracked throughout 2026. Earlier this year, Rio Tinto moved the final two ships from its eight-strong owned newcastlemax fleet, with Yasa Shipping taking RTM Drake and RTM Tasman . That completed a disposal programme which had earlier seen six other 205,000 dwt-class vessels leave the miner’s fleet. Rio Tinto’s latest marine figures show the mining giant operates more than 230 chartered vessels, moving more than 300m tonnes of cargo across roughly 2,700 voyages a year.

items.title: Premier Alliance prepares for Asia-N Europe services return to Suez
items.original_title: Premier Alliance prepares for Asia-N Europe services return to Suez
items.summary: October will see almost all global ocean carriers make a tentative return to Suez transits on Asia-Europe sailings, after revised pro forma shipping schedules show the Premier Alliance is set to send one of its vessels on the route through the Red Sea and Egyptian waterway. The schedule of the 8,100 teu One Continuity, published by Japanese carrier ONE, shows the vessel departing Laem Chabang on 19 October, after being reassigned to the Premier Alliance’s FE1 Asia-North Europe service. According to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, it has been deployed on ONE’s Asia-South America east coast SX1 service, operated in conjunction with Premier Alliance partners HMM and Yang Ming. According to the new FE1 pro forma, One Continuity will arrive at the Suez Canal on 9 November, and then at its first European port of call, Rotterdam, on 19 November. Other vessels in the FE1 service – the 9,000 teu NYK Venus , 8,200 teu ONE Hamburg , and 9,000 teu NYK Orion – are all also scheduled for Suez transits after leaving Asia in November and December. Meanwhile, Cosco vessels are also reportedly set to transit the Suez Canal, in the westbound direction, for the first time since the onset of the Red Sea Crisis, at the beginning of 2025.

items.title: EU’s need to raise steel output requires millions of tons of extra scrap: think tank
items.original_title: EU’s need to raise steel output requires millions of tons of extra scrap: think tank
items.summary: The EU must boost crude steel production 12%-13% by 2027 to counter falling imports triggered by steel safeguards and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, but meeting this target and rolling out new electric arc furnaces will require an additional 8 million-11 million metric tons of steel scrap later this decade, Stanislav Zinchenko, CEO of Kyiv-based think tank GMK Center, told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The EU was importing 7 million mt/year of long rolled steel before, with half of that tonnage produced via the blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace steelmaking route. Now, because of the safeguards and CBAM, this volume is likely to be replaced by EU-based scrap-intensive EAF production, he said. To replace the expected decline in steel imports, the required 12%-13% growth by 2027 in EU crude steel production, from 2025 levels, will need an extra 4 million-6 million mt of steel scrap. Then, by 2028, the commissioning of new EAFs could further boost domestic scrap demand by 4 million-5 million mt, according to Zinchenko.

items.title: Court Ruling: Part Of Taxonomy Criteria Found Unlawful – But Polluting Planes And Ships Still Slipping Through The Net
items.original_title: Court Ruling: Part Of Taxonomy Criteria Found Unlawful – But Polluting Planes And Ships Still Slipping Through The Net
items.summary: Yesterday, the General Court in Luxembourg has published its judgment on the EU Commission’s Taxonomy Regulations on ‘green’ investments for aviation and shipping. We welcome the Court’s finding that part of the shipping taxonomy criteria is unlawful. “We welcome the Court’s finding that part of the shipping Taxonomy criteria is unlawful, risking letting LNG-powered ships producing significant quantities of the super-pollutant methane be considered ‘green’ investments. However, the fact that methane slippage must now be quantified still gives the green light to label an entirely new fleet of cruise ships and airplanes as green, even though they will be fossil-fuelled for another 30 years. This means that EU climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra needs to ask himself: does he truly believe that it is a sustainable choice to invest in new fossil-fuelled cruise ships and aircrafts?” “We urge Wopke Hoekstra to follow up on his speech on doubling down on climate action after all the extreme weather events this summer, and reconsider the Taxonomy so it fulfils its intended purpose: drive the green transition through financial flows.” In August 2024, a coalition of NGOs took the EU Commission to court over its decision to include high-emitting fossil fuel planes and ships in the EU’s flagship sustainable finance legislation, the EU Taxonomy.

items.title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.original_title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.summary:
Poland's Supreme Administrative Court in Warsaw has dismissed a cassation appeal brought by the German environmental association Lebensraum Vorpommern against the planned deepwater container terminal in Świnoujście, the Szczecin and Świnoujście Seaports Authority announced. The appeal had challenged the project's environmental approvals through the Polish administrative courts, and its dismissal ends that line of litigation, removing one of the main legal obstacles to construction.

The terminal, now branded Cape Pomerania (Przylądek Pomorski), is designed to let the port handle the largest ocean-going container vessels and lift Poland's container capacity on the western coast. The court decision completes the environmental and administrative review process in the Polish judiciary. The announcement did not add new details on specifications, timetable or investment value beyond what the port authority has published before.
items.why: Removes a legal risk to the largest investment in the Szczecin–Świnoujście complex; expect the construction timetable, hinterland traffic and competitive landscape around Świnoujście to firm up.

items.title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.original_title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.summary:
The European Commission's July 2026 proposals would reshape the rules for maritime emissions, targeting a 90% cut in shipping greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. A new instrument, SMAP (Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion), would channel about EUR 15bn between 2028 and 2040 into clean fuels and propulsion.

From 2031 the EU ETS would extend to general cargo and offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnes, partly aligning with the UK ETS. The definition of offshore ship would move to an activity-based test, potentially capturing more vessels serving offshore wind farms. The separate ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime reporting systems would be merged into one compliance framework.

The package still needs agreement from the Council and Parliament, with political agreement targeted for Q1 2027 and implementation by 2029, and must be coordinated with the IMO Net Zero Framework.
items.why: Bringing 400–5,000 GT general cargo ships into the ETS raises costs for short-sea and feeder traffic calling at Baltic terminals; offshore-wind vessel rules touch Świnoujście's installation terminal.

items.title: Suez return could flip container shipping from shortage to surplus
items.original_title: Suez return could flip container shipping from shortage to surplus
items.summary:
Congestion currently absorbs about 1.7 million TEU of deep-sea container capacity, roughly 5% of the global fleet against a pre-pandemic 2.2%. Schedule reliability fell to 56.4% in July 2026, the year's low, with ships on average 6.06 days late.

As Asia–Europe services move back from the Cape of Good Hope to Suez, that tied-up capacity will be released; one service expects westbound transit to shorten by seven days and eastbound by 14. Around 1.5 million TEU is scheduled during China's Golden Week, 27% more than a year earlier, and Drewry expects 58 blank sailings out of 712 departures.

Rates are starting to soften: Drewry's World Container Index slipped 1% to USD 4,468 per 40-foot box, with a 14 million TEU newbuilding pipeline still to be delivered.
items.why: Falling container rates and more capacity can lower costs for shippers but pressure terminal and forwarding margins.

items.title: Dry bulk: Capesize near highs, Panamax firms, Supramax subdued (week to 25 Sept)
items.original_title: Dry bulk: Capesize near highs, Panamax firms, Supramax subdued (week to 25 Sept)
items.summary:
Capesize timecharter averages rose USD 142 week on week to USD 52,457 a day as Atlantic routes climbed on tight North Atlantic tonnage, though the C8 route eased more than USD 1,000 to USD 62,938 and Pacific rates softened.

Panamax and Kamsarmax rates strengthened in both basins; an 82,000-dwt trans-Atlantic round fixed at USD 21,300–22,400 and an Indonesia–India trip at USD 25,500.

Ultramax and Supramax markets were subdued by Asian holidays, slower North American demand and a lack of Mediterranean cargoes, although period interest continued for five- to 21-month terms. Handysize was firm in the Atlantic, helped by Mediterranean scrap demand; grain fixtures included a 38,000-dwt Recalada run at USD 29,500 and a 34,000-dwt US Gulf–Spain cargo at USD 25,000.
items.why: Freight levels for the handysize–panamax ships that carry grain, coal, steel and fertilisers into Baltic ports feed directly into cargo economics.

items.title: Uber Freight expands European 4PL business, plans Kraków hub in 2027
items.original_title: Uber Freight expands European 4PL business, plans Kraków hub in 2027
items.summary:
Uber Freight is expanding its fourth-party logistics (4PL) business in Europe, its biggest move on the continent since acquiring Transplace in 2021. Announced on 22 September from its Dutch base in Leusden, the plan includes a new Head of Europe role, investment in operations and its transport management system, and a second European hub and control tower in Kraków, Poland, in 2027.

The company says it doubled its count of new European 4PL deals in 2025, and chemical maker OXEA became its first 4PL customer spanning both North America and Europe. European road freight moved 13.3 billion tonnes in 2025, worth around EUR 440bn.
items.why: A tech-led 4PL competitor building presence in Poland could compete for freight-forwarding customers.

items.title: Ukraine weighs Baltic ports for grain as Black Sea disruption raises costs
items.original_title: Ukraine weighs Baltic ports for grain as Black Sea disruption raises costs
items.summary:
Ukraine's agriculture ministry is evaluating Baltic Sea ports as an alternative route for grain exports after attacks disrupted Black Sea shipping, which previously carried around 90% of Ukraine's exports. Grain is currently being redirected through three Danube ports, adding roughly USD 50 per tonne to logistics costs.

The Baltic route could in theory handle up to 20 million tonnes a year, but would add about USD 100 per tonne and would need around USD 2bn of international financial support. Because Ukraine has no border with the Baltic states, the cargo would have to transit Poland, where grain transit triggered farmer protests in 2022–2023.

In the first half of September around 340,000 tonnes moved by rail through Eastern European routes; only 65 of 278 daily grain wagons were heading to Poland.
items.why: A potential multi-million-tonne agri flow through Polish rail corridors and Baltic terminals; the agri segment is one of the group's stated 2026 growth priorities.

items.title: OT Logistics narrows H1 2026 net loss as EBITDA margin rises to 20%
items.original_title: OT Logistics narrows H1 2026 net loss as EBITDA margin rises to 20%
items.summary:
OT Logistics reported a consolidated net loss of PLN 6.25m for Q2 2026, compared with a PLN 9.98m loss a year earlier, and an operating profit (EBIT) of PLN 0.31m against a PLN 1.97m operating loss in Q2 2025. Q2 revenue rose to PLN 66.99m from PLN 63.18m.

For the first half of 2026 the group's net loss narrowed to PLN 11.53m from PLN 20.83m. Consolidated revenue fell to PLN 128.99m from PLN 135.17m, but EBITDA increased to PLN 26.17m from PLN 17.38m, lifting the EBITDA margin to 20.3% from 12.9%.

Port operations and rail segments grew, while freight forwarding revenue fell 22.7%. The company pointed to difficult market conditions affecting cargo flows and operational planning.
items.why: The group's own half-year results, as reported by the market; relevant for investor messaging and for benchmarking segments against peers.

items.title: PKP Cargo files creditor deal covering about EUR 690m of debt
items.original_title: PKP Cargo files creditor deal covering about EUR 690m of debt
items.summary:
PKP Cargo, Poland's largest rail freight operator, has submitted a restructuring arrangement proposal covering approximately EUR 690m of creditor debt, after repeated delays in agreeing terms. The proposal keeps the debt write-downs agreed earlier and adds a new element: creditors would share in any compensation recovered from PKP Cargo's claim of about EUR 350m against the Polish state.

The filing is a key step in the company's effort to avoid bankruptcy and complete its restructuring. Creditor acceptance is still needed, and part of the recovery for creditors depends on the outcome of the state claim.
items.why: The largest competitor and partner in Polish rail freight is still restructuring; its capacity and pricing affect port hinterland rail and the group's rail segment.

items.title: Carriers accelerate return to Suez despite new Red Sea risks
items.original_title: Carriers accelerate return to Suez despite new Red Sea risks
items.summary:
Container lines are speeding up their return to the Suez Canal. COSCO's 24,188-TEU OOCL Portugal made the line's first southbound transit since the Red Sea crisis began on 16 September 2026, and container ship net tonnage through the canal reached 72.1 million tons in the first eight months of 2026, up 54.2% year on year.

CMA CGM, Maersk, MSC, Hapag-Lloyd and COSCO have all resumed some Suez routings, and Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced four more Gemini Cooperation services moving back from the Cape of Good Hope.

Risks are rising, however: Houthi forces have captured Mocha and islands near the Bab el-Mandeb strait. They reportedly intend to keep earlier ceasefire commitments toward US and Israeli ships but reserve the right to target Saudi shipping. Both Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said continued Suez routing depends on Red Sea stability.
items.why: Shorter Asia–Europe transits change feeder schedules and container arrivals in Baltic ports; a reversal would hit them again.

items.title: Port Polska signs letter of intent for 25-hectare intermodal terminal near Kielce
items.original_title: Port Polska signs letter of intent for 25-hectare intermodal terminal near Kielce
items.summary:
Port Polska, the state infrastructure programme formerly known as CPK, has signed a letter of intent with the city of Kielce to develop a 25-hectare intermodal freight terminal in Obice, between Warsaw and Kraków. The terminal is intended to serve corridors to the Benelux, the Baltic states, Ukraine and Asia, including eastbound cargo and Europe–Asia routes.

Port Polska's Centre for Transport and Mobility will work with Kielce on analysing the impact on existing transport infrastructure. The delivery model, financing and construction schedule will be decided after those analyses. The wider Port Polska programme is budgeted at about PLN 130bn (EUR 31bn), mostly for a new airport and a high-speed rail network.
items.why: New inland intermodal capacity can redirect container and general-cargo flows between Polish seaports and the hinterland.

items.title: Maritime security: drone strike on Russia's Ust-Luga port, Hormuz threat 'extremely high'
items.original_title: Maritime security: drone strike on Russia's Ust-Luga port, Hormuz threat 'extremely high'
items.summary:
The weekly report recorded 22 maritime incidents worldwide. In the Baltic, a Ukrainian drone attack damaged oil-processing infrastructure at Russia's Ust-Luga port complex. In the Black Sea, Russian and Ukrainian forces struck cargo ships, tankers and support vessels almost daily near Yuzhny, Odesa, Sochi and Novorossiysk; the Russian-flagged Omskiy-107 caught fire and ran aground near Istanbul. Off Crete, the sanctioned ro-ro Lady Mariia was hit by about a dozen drones.

In the Strait of Hormuz, projectile strikes on tankers caused fatalities, US forces disabled three Iranian-linked tankers, Iran threatened a restricted navigation zone, and transits fell to their lowest level in months. The report rated Hormuz 'extremely high' and the Black Sea 'high' threat.
items.why: Attacks on Baltic energy ports and Black Sea shipping affect insurance, routing and which cargo shifts to Polish ports.

items.title: Poland reopens 'technical grain' probe as Ukraine seeks more transit via Polish ports
items.original_title: Poland reopens 'technical grain' probe as Ukraine seeks more transit via Polish ports
items.summary:
Poland and Ukraine are negotiating higher grain transit through Polish ports to Baltic destinations. Warsaw has acknowledged Kyiv's requests but remains cautious about straining port infrastructure; Polish ports can reportedly handle more than 1 million tonnes of agricultural products a month, with some spare capacity for Ukrainian cargo.

The talks have revived scrutiny of so-called technical grain imported in 2022–2023. A regional prosecutor's investigation, extended to 24 September 2026, is examining wheat, maize, rapeseed and soybeans declared for technical use that may have entered food and feed markets. According to Poland's Supreme Audit Office, about 103,000 tonnes of technical grain and 126,100 tonnes of technical rapeseed were imported from Ukraine between January 2022 and April 2023.

Direct imports of some Ukrainian agricultural products into Poland remain banned, but transit is allowed.
items.why: Transit rules and political sensitivity will decide whether Ukrainian agri volumes reach Polish terminals; worth tracking ahead of any new transit agreement.

items.title: Intermodal reaches record 19.2% share of Polish rail freight in Q1 2026
items.original_title: Intermodal reaches record 19.2% share of Polish rail freight in Q1 2026
items.summary:
Polish railways carried about 790,000 TEU of intermodal traffic in the first quarter of 2026, a record 19.2% share of all rail freight. The article notes intermodal transport's advantages as road haulage faces rising costs and driver shortages, citing industry estimates that rail routes from Poland to Italy cut CO2 emissions by more than 80% compared with alternatives.

Further growth depends on continued investment in rail lines and terminals across the region.
items.why: Intermodal growth supports container and general-cargo hinterland traffic for Polish ports.
